name: Kilba
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 5 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Mu'azu, Mohammed Aminu. 2009. Descriptive analysis of the Kilba tonal system. California Linguistic Notes 34(1), Winter 2009: 1-15. (Publisher PDF, CSU Fullerton CLN, via the Internet Archive copy ofhttp://hss.fullerton.edu/linguistics/cln/W09PDF/Muaza-KILBA%20TONAL%20SYSTEM%20_2_.pdf;author line 'Mohammed Aminu Muazu, University of Maiduguri'.)
catalog_locator: p. 2 (sec. I Introduction, last paragraph); p. 3 (sec. 4 'Tonal system in Kilba words', opening paragraph and minimal pairs); pp. 4-6 (tone patterns of monosyllabic, disyllabic and polysyllabic words, exx. 1a-1c); p. 6 (sec. 5 'Change of tone in Kilba verbs'); p. 7 (Katamba 1993 paraphrase, the only occurrences of 'stress').
catalog_quote: [p. 2] Having introduced the above terms, it is important to note that Kilba, like many African languages, is a tonal language. i.e., Each syllable in a Kilba word or sentence has its pitch, and this pitch is as much an essential element of that syllable as its consonant(s) and vowel(s). [p. 3] Kilba is a register tone language whereby the pitch height of the voice from syllable to syllable is phonologically contrastive. Kilba has two underlying tones namely: high (H, marked with acute accent, as in á) and low (L, marked with grave accent, as in à). As for contour tones, only the falling occurs in underlying representation. The falling tone may be analyzed as a sequence of high plus low on adjacent tone bearing units. Falling contour tone has ^ as in â. How important tone is in Kilba may be shown by the following short collection of pairs of words of different meanings, whose sounds (vowels and consonants) are differentiated by tones only: sà “to drink” sá “to lose” tà “stomach” tá “to cook” ... [p. 6] In a nutshell, we can categorically state that 90% of Kilba words or lexical items tones are L, LL, LLL and LLLL.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kilba is described as a two-tone register language (H, L, plus a falling contour) with lexically contrastive pitch on every syllable; the description contains no statement about word stress or accent placement.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress; the article notes some tonal changes under suffixation that do not fit its autosegmental account (p. 14).
new_statements.domain_note: Tone is stated for syllables in both words and sentences; minimal pairs are citation forms of nouns and verbs (mono-, di-, polysyllabic). No stress domain is discussed because no stress is described.
new_statements.identity_note: Huba = Kilba = Həba/Kəlba [hbb], glottocode huba1236 (Glottolog aliases Chobba, Hildi, 'Marghi South'; dialect 'Nya Huba'). Mu'azu's data and Schuh's informants are from Hong (Hong dialect, Adamawa State); Mu'azu 2009d treats Hong and Gaya as the two main dialects, differing only lexically and in a few consonants. Not to be confused with Margi South [mfm] or Kiluba (WALS 'kil').

sources.note: Kilba is a register tone language with two underlying tones H and L plus a falling contour (p. 3); every syllable of a word or sentence carries a pitch (p. 2). No statement about word stress at all; the word 'stress' appears only inside a quoted passage from Katamba (1993) on autosegmental tiers (pp. 7-8).

sources.citation: Kraft, Charles H. 1981. Chadic Wordlists, Volume II ("Biu-Mandara"). (Marburger Studien zur Afrika- und Asienkunde, Serie A: Afrika, 24.) Berlin: Dietrich Reimer. 199 pp. [Kilba list p. 88 ff. (page per the ASJP source note); Kilba rows digitised in the Lexibank CLDF dataset lexibank/kraftchadic, CC-BY-4.0]
sources.note: Primary tone-marked lexical data, no prose analysis: 431 of the 437 Kilba forms carry pitch diacritics. Kraft writes three pitch heights (acute 484 tokens, grave 464, macron 123, the macron almost only on vowels) plus contours (circumflex = falling, 26 tokens; caron on a vowel = rising, only c. 13 tokens: 107 of the 120 carons sit on c, r, s, j, z and are segmental haceks, not tone marks), e.g. ātsátǜ 'weave', àčíǹdá 'wash' (č = affricate). Raw phonetic evidence against which Mu'azu's two-tone (H, L + falling) analysis can be checked; no phonemic claim.
